# m100-silicon-binning

> An open-source analysis pipeline that recovers **per-die CPU core-harvesting maps** from
> out-of-band BMC/IPMI telemetry. Processor vendors fuse off defective units and sell the
> remainder as a lower-core-count part; which units they fused is proprietary. This project shows
> the telemetry supercomputers already collect discloses it, and recovers the map for all 1,962
> POWER9 sockets of CINECA's Marconi100 from a public dataset.

## What it is

- m100-silicon-binning is an open-source analysis pipeline for recovering per-die CPU
  core-harvesting maps from out-of-band BMC telemetry.
- It helps HPC operators and systems researchers see which cores a vendor fused off each
  individual processor die — information vendors do not publish.
- Use it when you have per-core sensor telemetry and want to audit procurement homogeneity, detect
  processor replacements without an asset database, or identify field core-guard events.
- It differs from PUF and hardware-fingerprinting work because it does not identify *which die* a
  part is; it recovers *what was disabled on it*, with no designed-in circuitry and no physical
  access.
- It is NOT a tool for reclaiming idle CPU cycles — that is the unrelated architectural sense of
  "core harvesting" — and it needs per-core sensors that expose physical position, which not every
  BMC does.

## How it works

A baseboard management controller exposes one thermal sensor per PHYSICAL core position and does
not renumber the surviving cores compactly. A core fused off at manufacture never emits a sample.
So the set of `pX_coreY_temp` metrics that report IS the die's harvest map. If a BMC renumbered
survivors, every socket would report indices 0-15 and there would be one pattern; instead 443 of
495 possible patterns occur.

## Key findings

- Harvesting operates exactly at the POWER9 slice (a core pair sharing L2/L3): 1,962 of 1,962
  sockets, zero exceptions in 1.67 million socket-days.
- The map is per-die, not per-SKU: 443 of 495 possible patterns observed.
- The sensor index IS the physical die ordering, recovered from thermal coupling alone: a 1x12
  linear arrangement fits at -0.791 against a random-ordering null of +0.001 +/- 0.121 (z = -6.55).
- Harvested slices cluster spatially: exactly eight positive-excess pairs at |dk| <= 2 in every run.
- A procurement-lot boundary at rack 22, permutation-calibrated p < 2.5e-4, assigning unseen racks
  to the correct delivery 95.9% of the time.
- Configuration changes coincide with reboots, measured against an independent boot signal:
  126 of 132 transitions, versus 1.74% of controls.
- Annualised socket replacement rate of 2.1% (95% CI [1.7, 2.6]) recovered with no asset database.
- The map does NOT predict which dies get replaced: out-of-fold C-index 0.448 against a
  permutation null of 0.499 +/- 0.031.
- Its effect on socket power is bounded, not negligible: +7.9 W over the feature range,
  90% CI [+0.9, +16.6], against a +/-5 W margin.

## Cost of the disclosure, and what mitigates it

Exact recovery from a SINGLE 20-second sampling interval for 99.7% of sockets. The knee is about
seven samples per core, roughly two minutes of telemetry. There are no false positives, because a
harvested core can never emit a sample.

Mitigations that do NOT work: reducing sampling cadence (recovery stays at 1.000 down to one sample
per core per day); dropping samples at random (still 1.000 after discarding 99.9%).
Mitigations that DO work: publishing per-socket aggregates instead of per-core series; renumbering
survivors compactly to 0..n-1. The channel is carried by which sensors EXIST, not by what they
report.

## Limitations

- Single system. Every result comes from Marconi100. Generalisation is untested and is the largest
  open weakness.
- Defect-driven versus policy-driven harvesting is NOT identified: both predict the clustering
  observed, and the fitted model cannot attribute it. The model is also misspecified.
- The lot boundary has no external confirmation from procurement records.
- The reliability null is bounded, not absolute: 92 events cannot exclude a small effect.
- The novelty statement is an awareness claim, not a priority claim.
